pages.description: Adjustments to how content is presented, how learners respond, or how the learning environment is structured that remove barriers for learners with disabilities or other access needs without changing the learning goal.
pages.title: Accommodations

pages.description: is the execution phase of a challenge-based or inquiry cycle, where learners move from investigation and planning into producing, testing, sharing, or implementing a response in the real world.
pages.title: Act

pages.description: Learners physically enact a concept, process, scenario, or role, converting verbal content into embodied performance.
pages.title: Act It Out

pages.description: Learners are encouraged to recall and activate prior knowledge to prepare for new learning.
pages.title: Activation

pages.description: Adaptive difficulty adjusts task challenge in response to learner performance so work remains demanding enough to promote growth without becoming discouraging or trivial.
pages.title: Adaptive Difficulty

pages.description: Adaptive learning tailors content, pacing, support, or task sequence in response to evidence about a learner's current performance, needs, or prior knowledge.
pages.title: Adaptive Learning

pages.description: Learners progress through levels of difficulty with personalized challenges and just-in-time feedback.
pages.title: Adaptive Mastery Learning

pages.description: Students of all ages carry misleading or outright wrong prior beliefs into a lesson, some well-documented and predictable, others idiosyncratic — anticipating them in advance and treating them with respect even while correcting them is more effective than assuming a blank slate.
pages.title: Addressing Student Misconceptions

pages.description: Concept maps, outlines, or visual guides that help learners structure new information before instruction.
pages.title: Advance Organizers

pages.description: A set of four proactive roles — active researcher/consumer, analyst, author, and socio-scientific communicator — that learners can take up when engaging with real-world data, rather than being positioned as passive recipients of official data.
pages.title: Agentic Data-Engagement Positions

pages.description: Analogies connect a new idea to a more familiar situation, structure, or experience so learners can reason about the unfamiliar in terms they already understand.
pages.title: Analogies

pages.description: Uses comparisons to familiar concepts to support understanding.
pages.title: Analogies and prior knowledge activation

pages.description: Anchored instruction situates learning around a shared, meaningful scenario or \"anchor\" that gives learners a concrete context for inquiry, analysis, and problem solving.
pages.title: Anchored Instruction

pages.description: The ABC model analyzes behavior as an environmental trigger (antecedent) producing an observable action (behavior) followed by an outcome that strengthens or weakens its recurrence (consequence) — the applied-behavior-analysis framework for identifying what is actually maintaining a classroom behavior before intervening.
pages.title: Antecedent-Behavior-Consequence (ABC) Model

pages.description: Learners actively apply knowledge in meaningful tasks.
pages.title: Application

pages.description: Learners apply concepts to real-world problems or case studies.
pages.title: Application of Knowledge

pages.description: Learners develop structured arguments with supporting evidence.
pages.title: Argument Construction

pages.description: Learners construct logical, evidence-based arguments to support their claims.
pages.title: Argumentation

pages.description: Learners verbalize their thought processes and reasoning, making their understanding — and misunderstandings — observable and open to refinement.
pages.title: Articulation

pages.description: Measures learner progress and determines mastery of content.
pages.title: Assess performance

pages.description: Assessment is the structured collection of evidence about learner understanding, performance, or progress for the purposes of feedback, decision making, grading, or revision.
pages.title: Assessment

pages.description: Learners are assigned a specific stance on an issue and must argue from that perspective.
pages.title: Assigned Positions

pages.description: Learners engage with pre-selected texts, articles, or book chapters to build foundational knowledge before or during instruction.
pages.title: Assigned Readings

pages.description: The design of instruction to capture, direct, and sustain learners' limited attentional resources toward content that matters for learning.
pages.title: Attention

pages.description: A front-end design activity that identifies learners' prior knowledge, characteristics, needs, and context so instruction can be matched to who will actually learn from it.
pages.title: Audience Analysis

pages.description: Audiobooks deliver text content through spoken audio, allowing learners to access material through listening rather than (or alongside) reading.
pages.title: Audiobooks

pages.description: Automaticity is the state in which a skill or recognition process executes with minimal conscious attention and working-memory demand, freeing cognitive resources for higher-level tasks.
pages.title: Automaticity

pages.description: Belonging is learners' perception of being accepted, valued, and socially connected within a learning community; it functions as a motivational precondition that designs must actively cultivate.
pages.title: Belonging

pages.description: Learners analyze real-world scenarios to apply theoretical concepts.
pages.title: Case-Based Learning

pages.description: Case studies are the element in which learners analyze a concrete scenario, incident, or example in order to reason about concepts, decisions, or consequences.
pages.title: Case Studies

pages.description: Learners analyze a real or hypothetical scenario to apply concepts.
pages.title: Case Study

pages.description: Challenge identification is the element in which learners or instructors surface the central obstacle, tension, or problem to be addressed.
pages.title: Challenge Identification

pages.description: A brief, structured interaction that surfaces learners' current understanding, emotional state, or progress so instruction can be adjusted in response.
pages.title: Check In

pages.description: Child-directed speech — exaggerated pitch, careful articulation, and simplified structure used when speaking with infants and toddlers — increases infant attention and supports early phoneme discrimination.
pages.title: Child-Directed Speech

pages.description: A choice board is a visual matrix of learning activities from which learners select a required subset, offering structured autonomy over how they practice and demonstrate learning.
pages.title: Choice Boards

pages.description: Structured conversations where learners analyze and reflect on content.
pages.title: Class Discussion

pages.description: Instructors provide individualized, ongoing support and guidance as learners perform a task, offering hints, feedback, and modeling tailored to current performance.
pages.title: Coaching

pages.description: Cognitive apprenticeship is the element in which learners observe expert thinking, practice with coaching, and gradually assume more responsibility.
pages.title: Cognitive Apprenticeship

pages.description: Deliberately introduces contradictions or challenges to a learner's existing knowledge to provoke deeper reasoning.
pages.title: Cognitive Conflict

pages.description: Cognitive load management is the element in which instruction is designed to reduce unnecessary processing and preserve effort for learning-relevant work.
pages.title: Cognitive Load Management

pages.description: Cognitive strategies are deliberate mental procedures — rehearsal, elaboration, organization, and monitoring — that learners use to select, construct, and retain information.
pages.title: Cognitive Strategies

pages.description: Collaboration is the short-form canonical target for learners working together toward a shared product, understanding, or decision.
pages.title: Collaboration

pages.description: Collaborative decision-making is the element in which learners evaluate options together and negotiate a shared choice or recommendation.
pages.title: Collaborative Decision-Making

pages.description: Collaborative discussion is the element in which learners build understanding together through shared talk, comparison of ideas, and negotiated meaning.
pages.title: Collaborative Discussion

pages.description: Collaborative inquiry is the element in which learners investigate a question together through shared sensemaking and evidence use.
pages.title: Collaborative Inquiry

pages.description: Learners work in structured teams to solve problems and complete tasks.
pages.title: Collaborative Learning

pages.description: Learners work together in small groups to analyze an authentic problem, negotiate meaning, and construct a shared solution.
pages.title: Collaborative Problem-Solving

pages.description: Communication channels are the element in which learners use designated tools or spaces to coordinate, discuss, ask questions, and share updates during a learning activity.
pages.title: Communication Channels

pages.description: Comparing cases is the element in which learners inspect two or more examples, solutions, texts, or scenarios side by side in order to notice meaningful similarities, differences, and governing principles.
pages.title: Comparing Cases

pages.description: Competency-based learning is the element in which progression is organized around demonstrated competence rather than seat time.
pages.title: Competency-Based Learning

pages.description: A concept map is a node-and-link diagram that externalizes relationships among ideas, making the structure of a knowledge domain visible.
pages.title: Concept Map

pages.description: Concept mapping is the element in which learners represent concepts and their relationships visually, typically as nodes and labeled links.
pages.title: Concept Mapping

pages.description: A multiple-choice question targeting a single conceptual difficulty, used with student voting and peer discussion to expose and confront misconceptions.
pages.title: ConcepTest

pages.description: Conceptual overviews are elements that present the broad structure, central idea, or organizing logic of a topic before moving into details.
pages.title: Conceptual Overviews

pages.description: Learners answer thought-provoking questions designed to challenge assumptions and deepen understanding.
pages.title: Conceptual Questioning

pages.description: Conceptual scaffolding is the element in which learners are given temporary structures, prompts, or representations that help them understand the underlying ideas of a domain before handling them independently.
pages.title: Conceptual Scaffolding

pages.description: Concrete modeling is the element in which physical or tangible representations are used to make abstract relationships visible.
pages.title: Concrete Modeling

pages.description: Structured group work in which learners negotiate, defend, and refine differing viewpoints to arrive at a shared conclusion.
pages.title: Consensus Building

pages.description: Learners work collaboratively to agree on a shared perspective or decision.
pages.title: Consensus Discussion

pages.description: Completion, short-answer, and extended-response (essay) items ask students to recall and produce an answer rather than recognize one, reducing guessing but introducing a genuine scoring-reliability problem that model answers, sample-reading, and rubrics are all meant to address.
pages.title: Constructed-Response Assessment Items

pages.description: Contextualization is the element in which new ideas, texts, or tasks are framed within a meaningful situation, purpose, domain, or prior experience.
pages.title: Contextualization

pages.description: Learning materials and concepts are revisited systematically to reinforce retention and prevent forgetting.
pages.title: Continuous Review

pages.description: Learners work in small structured groups toward shared goals, with positive interdependence and individual accountability built into the task design.
pages.title: Cooperative Learning

pages.description: Create a low-stress environment is the element of designing routines, norms, and spaces that reduce unnecessary anxiety during learning.
pages.title: Create a Low-Stress Environment

pages.description: Create a relaxed learning environment is the element of arranging social and physical conditions that support safety, calm, and participation.
pages.title: Create a Relaxed Learning Environment

pages.description: Creating visual representations is the element in which learners externalize understanding through diagrams, sketches, models, or other visuals.
pages.title: Creating Visual Representations

pages.description: Learners create rubrics or evaluation frameworks for assessment.
pages.title: Criteria Development

pages.description: Data analysis is the element in which learners inspect, interpret, organize, or transform data in order to answer questions, identify patterns, or justify conclusions.
pages.title: Data Analysis

pages.description: Debate is the element in which learners take positions, justify them with evidence, and respond to alternatives in a structured exchange.
pages.title: Debate

pages.description: A structured reflective conversation after an experience (simulation, discussion, case, or task) in which learners examine what happened, why, and what it means for future performance.
pages.title: Debrief

pages.description: Debriefing is the element in which learners reflect on an activity, simulation, or performance to consolidate what happened and why.
pages.title: Debriefing

pages.description: Learners evaluate options and make informed choices within a structured learning activity.
pages.title: Decision-Making

pages.description: A demonstration presents a complete or partial model of a skill, process, or solution so learners can observe expert performance before attempting it themselves.
pages.title: Demonstration

pages.description: An interactive shared-reading method in which an adult prompts children with questions, expands their responses, and gives feedback, turning storybook reading into a dialogue that builds expressive language.
pages.title: Dialogic Reading

pages.description: Learners take on distinct, interdependent roles within collaborative work to enhance accountability, engagement, and role-specific expertise.
pages.title: Differentiated Team Roles

pages.description: Digital learning is the element in which instruction, resources, or interaction are mediated through digital tools, platforms, or networks.
pages.title: Digital Learning

pages.description: Digital Open Badges are portable, metadata-rich micro-credentials that recognize discrete competencies, including informal learning that traditional grades and degrees do not capture or make transparent.
pages.title: Digital Open Badges

pages.description: Digital tools are the element in which learners use software, platforms, or digital applications to create, collaborate, practice, or receive feedback.
pages.title: Digital Tools

pages.description: Presents new content through explicit explanations, lectures, or demonstrations, with structured guidance before independent practice.
pages.title: Direct instruction

pages.description: Discrepant events are demonstrations, observations, or scenarios that violate learner expectations in a noticeable way.
pages.title: Discrepant Events

pages.description: Discussion is a structured verbal exchange in which learners articulate, question, and build on ideas together to construct and refine understanding.
pages.title: Discussion

pages.description: Discussion-based learning is the element in which talk, interpretation, and response are central vehicles for learning.
pages.title: Discussion-Based Learning

pages.description: A structured question or statement that initiates meaningful conversation among learners.
pages.title: Discussion Prompt

pages.description: Smaller, instructor- or TA-led sessions where learners analyze and discuss course material in depth.
pages.title: Discussion Sections

pages.description: Drill and practice is the element in which learners repeatedly perform a focused skill or response pattern until it becomes more fluent or automatic.
pages.title: Drill & Practice

pages.description: Dual coding is the element in which verbal and visual representations are used together to support understanding and memory.
pages.title: Dual Coding

pages.description: Elaboration asks learners to connect new material to prior knowledge by generating explanations, examples, analogies, or associations beyond what was presented.
pages.title: Elaboration

pages.description: Encourages learners to express their ideas, reasoning, and problem-solving approaches verbally.
pages.title: Eliciting Student Thinking

pages.description: An iterative formative-assessment task in which learners collaboratively choreograph movement to represent a concept, then revise it across cycles of peer feedback and reflection.
pages.title: Embodied Choreographic Assessment

pages.description: Instructional supports that help learners monitor, reframe, and manage emotional states — anxiety, boredom, frustration, and stress — so that affect does not consume cognitive and motivational resources needed for learning.
pages.title: Emotion Regulation

pages.description: Engage is the element in which instruction opens with an activity or prompt that draws attention and establishes interest.
pages.title: Engage

pages.description: Helps learners apply knowledge to new contexts through reflection and extension activities.
pages.title: Enhance retention and transfer

pages.description: Five recurring, teachable interaction moves — knowledge sharing, perspective-taking, simulation, knowledge validation, and negotiation — that interdisciplinary teams use to construct a shared problem understanding.
pages.title: Epistemic Games: Shared-Understanding Moves

pages.description: A simplified version of the full concept is introduced first before elaborating on details.
pages.title: Epitome (Elaboration Theory)

pages.description: Erroneous examples are worked examples that intentionally contain a mistake for learners to identify, explain, and correct.
pages.title: Erroneous Examples

pages.description: A task in which learners judge competing explanations for a phenomenon (mechanistic, circular, teleological), decide whether each actually answers a "how" question, and justify their evaluation.
pages.title: Evaluating and Justifying Mechanistic Explanations

pages.description: Learners evaluate competing models based on real-world evidence and refine their understanding.
pages.title: Evidence-Based Reasoning

pages.description: An example problem pair presents a fully worked solution followed immediately by a similar problem for the learner to solve, alternating study of an example with practice on an isomorphic task.
pages.title: Example Problem Pairs

pages.description: An exemplar is a high-quality model of a finished product or performance — an essay, design, proof, or solution — that learners study to internalize quality criteria before producing their own work.
pages.title: Exemplars

pages.description: Short bouts of physical activity inserted into instruction to restore attention, support memory consolidation, and improve on-task behavior.
pages.title: Exercise Breaks

pages.description: Learners form predictions, manipulate variables, and test hypotheses against observed outcomes rather than receiving conclusions directly.
pages.title: Experimentation

pages.description: Learners become subject-matter experts on one segment of a topic and teach that segment to peers, distributing expertise across the group.
pages.title: Expert Groups

pages.description: Expert modeling is the element in which a skilled performer demonstrates not only what to do, but how an expert notices cues, makes decisions, and checks quality during performance.
pages.title: Expert Modeling

pages.description: Explicit teaching is the element in which instructors directly explain, model, and sequence key knowledge or procedures rather than leaving them to be inferred.
pages.title: Explicit Teaching

pages.description: Fading is the element in which instructional support is deliberately reduced as learner competence grows.
pages.title: Fading

pages.description: Fading scaffolding is the element in which supports such as hints, prompts, or models are progressively reduced so that learners take on more of the task independently.
pages.title: Fading Scaffolding

pages.description: Learners receive input from instructors or peers to refine their work.
pages.title: Feedback

pages.description: A curated set of emotion words and phrases taught explicitly so learners can identify, label, and communicate internal states with precision.
pages.title: Feelings Vocabulary

pages.description: A cumulative assessment evaluating learners' mastery of the entire course material.
pages.title: Final Exam

pages.description: Flipped classroom is the element in which initial content exposure happens before class so in-class time can focus on application and feedback.
pages.title: Flipped Classroom

pages.description: Ongoing, low-stakes assessment to provide feedback and adjust instruction.
pages.title: Formative Assessment

pages.description: Engages learners with an unexpected event, question, or real-world scenario to capture focus.
pages.title: Gain attention

pages.description: Gamification is the element in which points, progress indicators, challenges, or other game-like structures are used to shape participation and persistence.
pages.title: Gamification

pages.description: Generation requires learners to produce an answer, word, rule, or representation themselves rather than passively reading or receiving it, strengthening memory and comprehension.
pages.title: Generation

pages.description: Learners construct their own understanding by actively generating connections, summaries, explanations, or representations rather than passively receiving material.
pages.title: Generative Processing

pages.description: Goal setting is the element in which learners or instructors establish clear targets for performance, progress, or improvement.
pages.title: Goal Setting

pages.description: Gradual release is the element in which responsibility for performance shifts from teacher or system to learner across stages of modeling, guided practice, and independent work.
pages.title: Gradual Release

pages.description: Graphic organizers are visual structures that help learners sort, compare, and connect ideas.
pages.title: Graphic Organizers

pages.description: A structured reflection in which cooperative groups evaluate how well they worked together and identify behaviors to keep or change.
pages.title: Group Processing

pages.description: Structured, assigned responsibilities within a small group that distribute the work of collaboration and make each member's contribution visible.
pages.title: Group Roles

pages.description: Group work is the element in which learners work together on a shared task, product, or problem.
pages.title: Group Work

pages.description: Guided discovery is the element in which learners investigate, infer, or notice patterns for themselves, but with prompts, constraints, examples, or feedback that keep the exploration productive.
pages.title: Guided Discovery

pages.description: Guided inquiry is the element in which learners investigate questions or problems with structured prompts, facilitator support, or staged resources that keep the inquiry productive.
pages.title: Guided Inquiry

pages.description: Guided practice is the element in which learners attempt a task with active support before moving to independent work.
pages.title: Guided Practice

pages.description: Hands-on learning is the element in which learners manipulate materials, tools, or environments directly while applying ideas in practice.
pages.title: Hands-on Learning

pages.description: Hints are partial prompts or cues that help learners continue a task without fully giving away the answer.
pages.title: Hints

pages.description: Learners explore interconnected digital content at their own pace.
pages.title: Hypertext Navigation

pages.description: Learners generate an explicit, testable prediction about an outcome or relationship, then confront evidence that confirms or disconfirms it.
pages.title: Hypothesis Testing

pages.description: Immediate feedback is the element in which response information is delivered close to the learner's action so it can still shape the next step.
pages.title: Immediate Feedback

pages.description: Learners engage in active, structured tasks during class to apply knowledge.
pages.title: In-Class Activities

pages.description: Learners work through material, tasks, or inquiry on their own, with responsibility for pacing, effort, and self-monitoring shifted from instructor to learner.
pages.title: Independent Study

pages.description: Individual accountability structures cooperative work so that each member's learning and contribution is separately assessed, preventing free-riding and ensuring every learner does the cognitive work.
pages.title: Individual Accountability

pages.description: Learners independently analyze their own thought processes, decisions, and learning experiences to build self-awareness and improve future performance.
pages.title: Individual Reflection

pages.description: Learners answer a question or solve a problem independently before group discussion.
pages.title: Individual Response

pages.description: Information literacy is the element in which learners identify information needs, locate sources, evaluate credibility, and use information responsibly.
pages.title: Information Literacy

pages.description: Learners investigate questions, problems, or phenomena — generating questions, gathering evidence, and drawing conclusions — rather than receiving explanations directly.
pages.title: Inquiry

pages.description: Learners investigate a topic through questioning, data gathering, and evidence evaluation to build understanding they construct rather than receive.
pages.title: Inquiry and Research

pages.description: Learners investigate open-ended problems and generate solutions.
pages.title: Inquiry-Based Exploration

pages.description: Inquiry-based learning is the element in which learners investigate questions, evidence, or problems in order to build understanding through guided exploration.
pages.title: Inquiry-Based Learning

pages.description: Learners investigate questions, generate or test hypotheses, and construct understanding through structured exploration rather than receiving explanations first.
pages.title: Inquiry Learning

pages.description: Learners reflect on and connect new learning to their own experiences, prior knowledge, and future applications.
pages.title: Integration

pages.description: An interview is a structured conversation in which learners pose questions to an expert, practitioner, community member, or peer to gather first-hand knowledge, perspectives, or data.
pages.title: Interviews

pages.description: An invention task asks learners to devise their own solution method or representation for a problem before receiving canonical instruction, preparing them to learn more deeply from subsequent teaching.
pages.title: Invention

pages.description: Investigate is the element in which learners collect information, examine evidence, or test ideas to answer a question.
pages.title: Investigate

pages.description: Iterative learning is the element in which learners improve through repeated cycles of attempt, feedback, revision, and retry.
pages.title: Iterative Learning

pages.description: Jigsaw is the element in which parts of a topic are distributed across learners who then teach one another to assemble the whole.
pages.title: Jigsaw

pages.description: Jigsaw learning is the short-form canonical target for the jigsaw-style distribution of expertise and peer teaching.
pages.title: Jigsaw Learning

pages.description: Journaling is the element in which learners record reflections, observations, questions, or progress over time in written form.
pages.title: Journaling

pages.description: Instruction is provided at the point of need rather than upfront.
pages.title: Just-in-Time Information

pages.description: Just-in-time learning is the element in which information, guidance, or resources are provided at the moment they are needed for the task at hand rather than front-loaded in advance.
pages.title: Just-in-Time Learning

pages.description: Justification is the element in which learners explain why a claim, choice, or solution is warranted using reasons, criteria, or evidence.
pages.title: Justification

pages.description: Learners defend conclusions with evidence and reasoning, constructing and critiquing arguments to build critical reasoning and conceptual understanding.
pages.title: Justification & Argumentation

pages.description: Knowledge-building is the element in which learners collectively construct, refine, and extend ideas rather than only consume or repeat them.
pages.title: Knowledge-Building

pages.description: Learners engage in structured discussions to deepen understanding.
pages.title: Knowledge-Building Discourse

pages.description: Learners integrate multiple perspectives and sources to develop a cohesive understanding.
pages.title: Knowledge Synthesis

pages.description: Learner choice is the element in which learners are given meaningful options about task, process, product, or pathway.
pages.title: Learner Choice

pages.description: Learning Analytics-Driven Feedback uses models built from learner interaction data to predict at-risk learners and surface targeted feedback to learners or instructors, compensating for the reduced visibility distance and online instructors have into struggling learners.
pages.title: Learning Analytics-Driven Feedback

pages.description: A learning contract is a negotiated written agreement in which a learner commits to specific goals, activities, resources, timelines, and evidence of accomplishment, typically with instructor sign-off.
pages.title: Learning Contracts

pages.description: Learning goals are explicit statements of what learners should know or be able to do after instruction, serving as the reference point for designing activities and assessments.
pages.title: Learning Goals

pages.description: Learning management systems are the element in which course organization, materials, communication, and tracking are coordinated through an LMS.
pages.title: Learning Management Systems

pages.description: Learning objectives are explicit statements of what learners should know or be able to do after instruction, providing direction for design, instruction, and assessment.
pages.title: Learning Objectives

pages.description: Learning outcomes are explicit statements of what learners should know, understand, or be able to do by the end of an instructional experience.
pages.title: Learning Outcomes

pages.description: A learning task is the integrated, meaningful unit of work — a problem, project, case, or performance — that learners undertake to acquire knowledge and skill in context.
pages.title: Learning Tasks

pages.description: A lecture is an instructor-led, largely one-to-many presentation of content in spoken (often supplemented by visual) form, delivering explanation, narrative, and worked reasoning to a group.
pages.title: Lecture

pages.description: Instructor-led presentation of content in a structured format.
pages.title: Lectures

pages.description: A multimodal reflection protocol in which learners individually record noticings in whatever mode feels natural (words, sketches, gesture, movement), then build a collaborative representation with peers before sharing with the whole group.
pages.title: Listening Palette

pages.description: Literature review is the element in which learners gather, evaluate, and synthesize existing sources on a topic in order to understand the current state of knowledge or argument.
pages.title: Literature Review

pages.description: A Makerspace is a physical or mobile space, formal or informal, where learners use digital and physical tools to design, build, and iterate on self-directed projects.
pages.title: Makerspace

pages.description: Mastery learning is the element in which progression depends on demonstrated understanding rather than time alone.
pages.title: Mastery Learning

pages.description: Learners cannot advance until they demonstrate mastery of foundational content.
pages.title: Mastery Progression

pages.description: A mental model is a learner's internal representation of how a system, process, or domain works, which they use to explain phenomena, predict outcomes, and reason about new situations.
pages.title: Mental Models

pages.description: Metacognition is the element in which learners monitor, explain, and regulate their own thinking.
pages.title: Metacognition

pages.description: Metacognitive reflection is the element in which learners examine how they thought, what strategies they used, where they were confused, and what they should do next.
pages.title: Metacognitive Reflection

pages.description: Metacognitive strategies are deliberate learner moves for planning, monitoring, checking, and revising thinking during learning.
pages.title: Metacognitive Strategies

pages.description: Metaphors are explanatory comparisons that map a less familiar concept onto a more familiar image or experience.
pages.title: Metaphors

pages.description: A summative assessment administered at the midpoint of a course to evaluate learning progress and retention of material covered to date.
pages.title: Midterm Exam

pages.description: A diagnostic question or task designed to surface learners' incorrect intuitions so they can be confronted and revised before instruction consolidates them.
pages.title: Misconception Probes

pages.description: Learners engage in a structured, goal-oriented challenge framed as a mission with a clear objective, constraints, and success criteria.
pages.title: Mission-Based Learning

pages.description: Learners refine their conceptual models based on evidence and feedback.
pages.title: Model Revision

pages.description: Instructors or advanced learners demonstrate expert thinking and behavior so learners can observe expert performance before attempting it themselves.
pages.title: Modeling

pages.description: An instructor or facilitator guides discussions to ensure productive engagement.
pages.title: Moderation

pages.description: Multimedia instruction is the element in which teaching combines spoken or written language with visuals, diagrams, animation, or other media in a coordinated instructional sequence.
pages.title: Multimedia Instruction

pages.description: Multimedia learning is the element in which learners engage with coordinated combinations of words, visuals, audio, animation, or interactive media.
pages.title: Multimedia Learning

pages.description: Multimedia projects are the element in which learners create artifacts that combine text, visuals, audio, video, or interaction.
pages.title: Multimedia Projects

pages.description: Negotiation is the element in which learners work through competing interests, priorities, or interpretations in order to reach a decision, compromise, or shared position.
pages.title: Negotiation

pages.description: Non-examples are intentionally chosen instances that do not meet the target concept, criterion, or quality standard.
pages.title: Non-Examples

pages.description: Note-taking is the element in which learners record, organize, and condense information in ways that support later understanding and retrieval.
pages.title: Note-Taking

pages.description: An objective is an explicit statement of what learners should know or be able to do after instruction, serving as the design anchor for activities, materials, and assessment.
pages.title: Objective

pages.description: Observation is the short-form canonical target for instructional activities in which learners watch people, processes, or contexts carefully in order to notice patterns, behaviors, or constraints.
pages.title: Observation

pages.description: Learners observe a live or recorded performance by an expert or peer, then immediately imitate or "shadow" that performance themselves.
pages.title: Observation Shadowing

pages.description: Observation/shadowing is the element in which learners watch practice in context in order to notice decisions, routines, and tacit moves before attempting similar work themselves.
pages.title: Observation/Shadowing

pages.description: Open Educational Resources are teaching materials licensed to grant free, perpetual permission to retain, reuse, revise, remix, and redistribute them — the "5Rs" test that distinguishes genuine open licensing from merely free-to-enroll access.
pages.title: Open Educational Resources (The 5Rs)

pages.description: Facilitated dialogue where learners explore topics without predetermined answers.
pages.title: Open-Ended Discussion

pages.description: Supplementary activities designed to reinforce learning and provide formative feedback.
pages.title: Optional Quizzes or Discussion Sections

pages.description: Isolated, repeated practice of elements that require automation for efficient task performance.
pages.title: Part-task practice

pages.description: A discourse move in which a learner positions themselves as a character within a case or example under academic study, using the case to reason about their own identity category membership rather than only about the case's distant subject.
pages.title: Participant Examples

pages.description: An embodied on-screen agent that points and gazes directly at feedback text when it appears, using social cueing rather than a generic arrow to pull elementary students' attention to feedback they would otherwise skip.
pages.title: Pedagogical Agent Signaling for Feedback Salience

pages.description: Peer assessment is the element in which learners evaluate the work or reasoning of peers against shared criteria.
pages.title: Peer Assessment

pages.description: Learners work together to complete tasks or solve problems, negotiating meaning and distributing cognitive effort.
pages.title: Peer Collaboration

pages.description: Learners engage in structured conversations with classmates to explore, articulate, and refine ideas.
pages.title: Peer Discussion

pages.description: Learners verbalize their thinking to peers, strengthening their own understanding.
pages.title: Peer Explanation

pages.description: Peer feedback is the element in which learners respond to one another's work with comments intended to improve revision or performance.
pages.title: Peer Feedback

pages.description: Peer feedback/peer review is the element in which learners evaluate one another's work against criteria and provide revision-oriented feedback.
pages.title: Peer Feedback/Peer Review

pages.description: Peer instruction is the element in which learners explain, compare, and revise answers with one another around conceptual questions.
pages.title: Peer Instruction

pages.description: Learners engage with one another through discussions, debates, or collaborative tasks.
pages.title: Peer Interaction

pages.description: Peer review is the element in which learners examine and respond to one another's work using shared criteria, prompts, or examples.
pages.title: Peer Review

pages.description: Learners explain concepts to peers, reinforcing their own understanding.
pages.title: Peer Teaching

pages.description: Performance-based assessment is the element in which learners demonstrate knowledge or skill by performing, producing, or solving something observable rather than only selecting answers.
pages.title: Performance-Based Assessment

pages.description: Performance support provides task-specific guidance at the moment of need within the work context, reducing reliance on memorized knowledge.
pages.title: Performance Support

pages.description: Personalized pacing is the element in which learners move through content or practice at different rates based on need and progress.
pages.title: Personalized Pacing

pages.description: Learners deliberately consider multiple viewpoints on an issue to build cognitive flexibility, empathy, and deeper conceptual understanding.
pages.title: Perspective-Taking

pages.description: Learners develop techniques to convince others using logic and evidence.
pages.title: Persuasion

pages.description: Physical Education (PE) is a curricular domain in which learning goals — motor skill, tactical understanding, fitness, and dispositions — are achieved primarily through structured physical activity rather than text or discussion.
pages.title: Physical Education

pages.description: A portfolio is a purposeful, curated collection of learner work assembled over time, accompanied by reflection, used to document growth and assess competence.
pages.title: Portfolio

pages.description: Learners construct and refine a defensible stance on a contested issue through evidence-based reasoning and adversarial or dialogic testing.
pages.title: Position Development

pages.description: A structural condition in cooperative learning where group members cannot succeed unless all members succeed, linking individual outcomes to shared goals.
pages.title: Positive Interdependence

pages.description: Encourages learners to apply new knowledge or skills through structured activities.
pages.title: Practice

pages.description: Learners actively retrieve information from memory as a learning activity, rather than rereading or reviewing material.
pages.title: Practice Testing

pages.description: Pre-class preparation is the element in which learners engage with readings, videos, prompts, or other materials before a live class session so that class time can focus on discussion, application, or problem solving.
pages.title: Pre-Class Preparation

pages.description: Instructional content is delivered via video or recorded lecture before in-class activities, freeing class time for active learning.
pages.title: Pre-Class Video/Lecture

pages.description: Pre-reading activities are tasks completed before reading in order to activate prior knowledge, establish purpose, surface key vocabulary, or prepare attention for important ideas.
pages.title: Pre-Reading Activities

pages.description: Pre-reading questioning is the element in which learners preview a text through guiding questions before or during initial reading.
pages.title: Pre-Reading Questioning

pages.description: Learners review content before engaging in discussion-based activities.
pages.title: Pre-Seminar Preparation

pages.description: A prediction asks learners to commit to an answer or outcome before instruction, activating prior knowledge and creating a gap that subsequent teaching resolves.
pages.title: Prediction

pages.description: Prior knowledge activation is the element in which learners recall, surface, or organize what they already know before engaging with new material.
pages.title: Prior Knowledge Activation

pages.description: Probing uses targeted follow-up questions to push learners beyond initial answers, exposing reasoning, surfacing misconceptions, and deepening elaboration.
pages.title: Probing

pages.description: Problem-based learning, as an element, refers to the use of an authentic or ill-structured problem as the immediate driver of inquiry, information seeking, and solution development inside a larger design.
pages.title: Problem-Based Learning

pages.description: Learners are introduced to a real-world problem to analyze and solve.
pages.title: Problem Presentation

pages.description: Learners engage with a structured real-world scenario that requires problem-solving.
pages.title: Problem Scenario

pages.description: Problem scenarios are concrete situations presented to learners as the context for inquiry, analysis, or solution development.
pages.title: Problem Scenarios

pages.description: Problem solving is the element in which learners identify, analyze, and respond to a challenge by generating and evaluating possible solutions.
pages.title: Problem Solving

pages.description: Learners complete structured activities that require critical thinking and application.
pages.title: Problem-Solving Tasks

pages.description: Step-by-step instructions and just-in-time guidance to assist learners in acquiring procedural fluency.
pages.title: Procedural Information

pages.description: Procedural learning is the element in which learners acquire stepwise routines, methods, or operations through guided performance.
pages.title: Procedural Learning

pages.description: A product is the tangible artifact or performance a learner creates to demonstrate learning — the observable output that anchors assessment, feedback, and transfer.
pages.title: Product

pages.description: Progress tracking is the element in which learners or instructors monitor advancement through goals, tasks, competencies, or milestones over time.
pages.title: Progress Tracking

pages.description: Progressive disclosure presents information in sequenced stages, revealing complexity only as the learner is ready, rather than showing everything at once.
pages.title: Progressive Disclosure

pages.description: Promote a sense of home is the element of creating belonging, familiarity, and social warmth within a learning environment.
pages.title: Promote a Sense of Home

pages.description: A prompt is a cue, question, or instruction embedded in a learning task that directs learner attention, elicits a response, or scaffolds a cognitive process at the moment it is needed.
pages.title: Prompts

pages.description: Gives learners corrective or reinforcing feedback to improve performance.
pages.title: Provide Feedback

pages.description: Offers scaffolding, modeling, or examples to support learning.
pages.title: Provide guidance

pages.description: A digital-environment design construct specifying five characteristics — consistent feedback, frequent failure tightly coupled to that feedback, non-standard representations, late or absent formal notation, and legitimate alternative solution paths — that together support productive mathematical play rather than frustration or rote procedure.
pages.title: Provocative Objects

pages.description: Placing related text and graphics close together on the page or screen so learners can process them as a single unit rather than searching and holding them in working memory.
pages.title: Proximity

pages.description: Public display is the element in which learner work is made visible to a wider audience in the classroom or beyond.
pages.title: Public Display

pages.description: Public product is the element in which learners create work intended for real audiences beyond the teacher alone.
pages.title: Public Product

pages.description: Public speaking is the element in which learners present ideas aloud to an audience with attention to clarity, organization, evidence, and delivery.
pages.title: Public Speaking

pages.description: Learners generate their own questions to guide inquiry.
pages.title: Question Formulation

pages.description: Short, low-stakes assessments that reinforce learning and provide feedback.
pages.title: Quizzes

pages.description: Real-world math is the element in which mathematical reasoning is embedded in practical or authentic contexts.
pages.title: Real-World Math

pages.description: Real-world problems are tasks framed around authentic issues, needs, or dilemmas outside purely academic abstraction.
pages.title: Real-World Problems

pages.description: Learners revisit and revise their responses after discussion or additional learning.
pages.title: Reassessment

pages.description: Learners counter opposing viewpoints with evidence-based arguments.
pages.title: Rebuttals

pages.description: Activates learners' existing mental models to connect new information.
pages.title: Recall prior knowledge

pages.description: Learners take turns leading structured dialogue — predicting, questioning, clarifying, and summarizing — to build comprehension of shared text or content.
pages.title: Reciprocal Teaching

pages.description: Learners analyze their experiences, actions, or decisions to deepen learning.
pages.title: Reflection

pages.description: Reflection activities are structured tasks that ask learners to examine what they did, understood, or would change next.
pages.title: Reflection Activities

pages.description: Reinforcement is the delivery of a consequence (reward, praise, feedback, or removal of an aversive condition) contingent on a learner's behavior, intended to increase the frequency or persistence of that behavior.
pages.title: Reinforcement

pages.description: Representational drawing is the element in which learners sketch, diagram, or draw structures and relationships to support understanding.
pages.title: Representational Drawing

pages.description: Learners conduct investigations to explore topics, gather evidence, and develop conclusions.
pages.title: Research

pages.description: Observation, surveys, and archival/content analysis are the main methods researchers use to gather data, each with a distinct tradeoff between ecological validity, depth, and cost that mirrors — but is methodologically distinct from — their use as classroom-assessment techniques.
pages.title: Research Data Collection Methods

pages.description: Learners assess the credibility and relevance of sources.
pages.title: Resource Evaluation

pages.description: Resource hubs are centralized collections of materials, links, tools, or references that learners can return to during a course or project.
pages.title: Resource Hubs

pages.description: Retrieval practice asks learners to actively recall information from memory rather than re-read or re-hear it, strengthening the memory trace each time it is accessed.
pages.title: Retrieval

pages.description: Retrieval practice is the element in which learners recall information from memory rather than only re-exposing themselves to it.
pages.title: Retrieval Practice

pages.description: Learners reflect on their own or peers' work before finalizing.
pages.title: Review

pages.description: Review and summarizing asks learners to re-engage with previously covered material by condensing it into their own words, consolidating memory and revealing gaps in understanding.
pages.title: Review And Summarizing

pages.description: Learners improve their work based on feedback and self-reflection.
pages.title: Revision

pages.description: Rhetorical strategies are deliberate moves learners use to persuade, frame, emphasize, appeal to an audience, or strengthen the force of an argument.
pages.title: Rhetorical Strategies

pages.description: Role-playing is the element in which learners adopt roles and act through a scenario, interaction, or decision process from that perspective.
pages.title: Role-Playing

pages.description: Learners switch sides in a debate or discussion to argue from the opposite perspective.
pages.title: Role Reversal

pages.description: A rubric is a scoring guide that makes evaluation criteria and performance levels explicit before learners attempt a task, supporting both assessment and self-regulation.
pages.title: Rubric

pages.description: Rubric design is the element in which criteria and performance levels are made explicit through a structured evaluative framework.
pages.title: Rubric Design

pages.description: Rubrics are the element in which criteria and performance levels are made explicit to guide quality work and evaluation.
pages.title: Rubrics

pages.description: Gradually shifts learners from guided exploration to independent inquiry.
pages.title: Scaffolded Inquiry

pages.description: Scaffolding is the element in which support is added temporarily so learners can perform tasks they could not yet complete independently.
pages.title: Scaffolding

pages.description: Scenario-based learning is the element in which instruction is organized around a realistic situation, case, or mission that requires learners to interpret information and make decisions in context.
pages.title: Scenario-Based Learning

pages.description: Scientific reasoning is the element in which learners generate explanations, evaluate evidence, test claims, and revise models using disciplinary norms of inquiry.
pages.title: Scientific Reasoning

pages.description: Multiple-choice, true-false, and matching items ask students to select rather than construct a response — easy to score objectively, but hard to write well, and appropriate mainly for recognition-level rather than complex learning goals.
pages.title: Selected-Response Assessment Items

pages.description: Self-assessment is the element in which learners judge their own work, understanding, or progress against explicit criteria.
pages.title: Self-Assessment

pages.description: A learner's belief in their own capability to organize and execute the actions required to perform a task, which strongly influences motivation, effort, persistence, and achievement.
pages.title: Self Efficacy

pages.description: Self-explanation is the element in which learners explain to themselves why something is true, why a step works, or how a solution fits the problem.
pages.title: Self-Explanation

pages.description: Self-monitoring is the element in which learners track their own attention, behavior, progress, or accuracy during learning.
pages.title: Self-Monitoring

pages.description: Self-paced learning is the element in which learners control the rate or sequence of progress through material within a designed structure.
pages.title: Self-Paced Learning

pages.description: The Self-Regulation Questionnaire is a 63-item self-report instrument, built on the Miller and Brown seven-step model of self-regulation, that scores a person's overall self-regulation capacity as high, moderate, or low.
pages.title: Self-Regulation Questionnaire (SRQ)

pages.description: Self-testing is the element in which learners quiz themselves or otherwise attempt to retrieve knowledge without immediate external prompting.
pages.title: Self-Testing

pages.description: Seminar format is the element in which learning is organized around sustained discussion of a shared text, question, or issue with facilitator support but strong learner participation.
pages.title: Seminar Format

pages.description: Sentence starters (or sentence frames) provide partial sentence openings that structure learner responses, reducing the language-generation burden so learners can focus on content and reasoning.
pages.title: Sentence Starters

pages.description: Shared documents are the element in which multiple learners contribute to a common editable artifact.
pages.title: Shared Documents

pages.description: Learning progresses from basic concepts to more detailed, complex ideas, so foundational knowledge is established before advanced material is introduced.
pages.title: Simple-to-complex sequencing

pages.description: A simulation is an interactive model of a system or environment in which learners act, observe consequences, and iterate, learning through controlled experimentation rather than direct instruction.
pages.title: Simulation

pages.description: Simulations are the element in which learners engage with realistic, model-based scenarios that approximate authentic systems or environments.
pages.title: Simulations

pages.description: Small-group instruction is the element in which learners work with an instructor or facilitator in a reduced-size group for targeted teaching, discussion, or support.
pages.title: Small-Group Instruction

pages.description: SMARTER goals are a structured goal-setting element that asks learners to define goals that are specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound, evaluated, and revised or rewarded, depending on the local formulation.
pages.title: SMARTER Goals

pages.description: Social learning is the element in which interaction with peers, models, or communities is treated as a direct source of learning.
pages.title: Social Learning

pages.description: Socratic questioning is the element in which prompts are used to probe assumptions, clarify reasoning, test evidence, and extend implications.
pages.title: Socratic Questioning

pages.description: Socratic seminar is the element in which learners build understanding through text-centered questioning and discussion.
pages.title: Socratic Seminar

pages.description: Learners synthesize information to propose and test solutions.
pages.title: Solution Development

pages.description: Spaced learning is the element in which practice or review is distributed over time rather than massed together.
pages.title: Spaced Learning

pages.description: Spaced repetition is the element in which key material is revisited at strategically increasing intervals rather than massed into a single session.
pages.title: Spaced Repetition

pages.description: A learning disability is a significant, specific gap between a student's ability and one narrow area of academic achievement (reading, writing, or math) that persists despite ordinary teaching effort and isn't explained by broader intellectual, sensory, or language-acquisition factors — with dyslexia, dysgraphia, and dyscalculia as the three most commonly diagnosed forms.
pages.title: Specific Learning Disabilities

pages.description: Spiral curriculum is the element in which important ideas are revisited repeatedly over time, with each return expanding complexity or depth.
pages.title: Spiral Curriculum

pages.description: Clearly communicates the learning goals to set expectations and focus attention.
pages.title: State objectives

pages.description: Structured academic controversy is the element in which learners argue multiple sides of an issue before synthesizing a shared conclusion.
pages.title: Structured Academic Controversy

pages.description: Structured debate is the element in which learners examine opposing claims using explicit roles, turn structures, evidence requirements, and response rules.
pages.title: Structured Debate

pages.description: Structured discussion is the element in which talk is guided by prompts, roles, turns, protocols, or evidence requirements rather than left entirely open.
pages.title: Structured Discussion

pages.description: Instructors guide learners with sequenced, purposeful questions to scaffold deeper inquiry.
pages.title: Structured Questioning

pages.description: Student-led IEPs place the student with a disability in the driver's seat of their own Individualized Education Program meeting — preparing, presenting, and negotiating goals with support from educators and family.
pages.title: Student-Led IEPs

pages.description: Learners submit work for assessment, feedback, or peer review at structured checkpoints.
pages.title: Submission

pages.description: Learners distill key concepts from a discussion, reading, or experience into their own condensed restatement or integrated account.
pages.title: Summarization and Synthesis

pages.description: Summative assessment is the element in which a learner's performance is judged at the end of a unit, course, or other instructional sequence.
pages.title: Summative Assessment

pages.description: Supportive information provides the cognitive strategies, mental models, and conceptual frameworks necessary for tackling complex tasks.
pages.title: Supportive information

pages.description: Task management is the element in which learners organize, track, assign, or sequence work across a project or collaborative activity.
pages.title: Task Management

pages.description: Students work in structured groups to analyze problems, construct solutions, and reflect together.
pages.title: Team-Based Inquiry

pages.description: Technology integration is the element in which digital tools are used in direct service of learning goals, feedback, access, or collaboration.
pages.title: Technology Integration

pages.description: A study aid involving marking text to indicate importance.
pages.title: Text underlining and annotating

pages.description: Think-aloud is the element in which an instructor, peer, or learner verbalizes reasoning while performing a task.
pages.title: Think-Aloud

pages.description: A transfer task requires learners to apply learned knowledge or skills to a novel problem or context different from the one in which they were taught.
pages.title: Transfer Tasks

pages.description: Video-based reflection is the element in which learners or practitioners review recorded performance to analyze choices, patterns, and next steps.
pages.title: Video-Based Reflection

pages.description: Video prompts are short video clips used to launch attention, curiosity, discussion, or analysis.
pages.title: Video Prompts

pages.description: Virtual whiteboards are the element in which learners sketch, annotate, and collaborate in a shared digital visual workspace.
pages.title: Virtual Whiteboards

pages.description: Visual imagery asks learners to form or use mental pictures — or supports them with concrete images — so that verbal content is encoded in both visual and verbal channels.
pages.title: Visual Imagery

pages.description: Learners present their ideas, responses, or conclusions to the entire class, often following small-group or pair work.
pages.title: Whole-Class Sharing

pages.description: Whole-task performance engages learners in authentic, complex tasks that integrate multiple skills and knowledge areas simultaneously, mirroring the conditions of real-world practice.
pages.title: Whole-task performance

pages.description: Worked examples are the element in which learners study complete or partial solutions before attempting similar problems independently.
pages.title: Worked Examples

pages.description: A writing prompt is a task specification that directs learners to produce written text — explaining, arguing, reflecting, or synthesizing — in order to consolidate and reveal understanding.
pages.title: Writing Prompts

pages.description: Whether a learner can perceive and operate the material at all — device, bandwidth, sensory and motor.
pages.title: Access

pages.description: What a learner does with frustration, anxiety and failure while the work is still in front of them.
pages.title: Affect Regulation

pages.description: How long a learner can sustain focus on one thing, and how easily something else takes it away.
pages.title: Attention

pages.description: Whether a learner expects to be treated as a full participant in this setting, and how much of their attention that question consumes.
pages.title: Belonging

pages.description: Whether a learner can operate the interface the instruction is delivered through, independently of whether they can reach it.
pages.title: Digital Literacy

pages.description: The sector, role or setting a scenario has to be placed in before a learner recognises it as their own.
pages.title: Domain Context

pages.description: Whether a learner is willing to spend effort here, and what makes the spending feel worth it.
pages.title: Motivation

pages.description: A learner's existing domain knowledge in the subject area before instruction begins.
pages.title: Prior Knowledge

pages.description: What a learner can read fluently, and whether the language of instruction is the one they think in.
pages.title: Reading and Language

pages.description: Whether a learner can plan, monitor and adjust their own work without the structure being supplied.
pages.title: Self-Regulation

pages.description: How much uninterrupted time a learner actually gets, and whether progress survives the gap until the next session.
pages.title: Time and Continuity

pages.description: How much a learner can hold and manipulate at once before the material itself becomes the obstacle.
pages.title: Working Memory

pages.description: Building learner personas and design scenarios around the activity system a learner acts within — object, mediating tools, rules, community and division of labour — so that the design responds to what constrains the learner rather than to who they are demographically.
pages.title: Activity-System Personas and Scenarios

pages.description: A curriculum planning strategy that begins by defining desired learning outcomes and acceptable evidence of achievement, then designs instruction last.
pages.title: Backward Design

pages.description: A family of interview and observation methods for eliciting the cues, judgements and decision rules an expert uses but cannot readily articulate — the tacit content that a procedural task analysis records as a single step.
pages.title: Cognitive Task Analysis

pages.description: A design process for building formative assessment tasks that reveal disciplinary competence (e.g., computational thinking) embedded in a specific community's everyday practices, by interviewing families to surface funds of knowledge before designing the task.
pages.title: Family-Interview-Based Assessment Task Design

pages.description: Systematically gathering information about learners' prior knowledge, skills, motivations, and constraints to inform instructional design decisions.
pages.title: Learner Analysis

pages.description: Systematic investigation of learners' prior knowledge, characteristics, and the instructional environment before designing instruction, so that design decisions fit who will learn and where.
pages.title: Learner And Context Analysis

pages.description: Learner personas are evidence-based composite profiles of representative learners used to ground design decisions in real audience characteristics.
pages.title: Learner Personas

pages.description: Task analysis identifies the prerequisite skills a target performance requires by repeatedly asking what a learner must already master, arranging the answers into a sequenced learning hierarchy from foundational to complex.
pages.title: Learning Hierarchy Task Analysis

pages.description: A design strategy that surfaces and names power dynamics among stakeholders, making decision-making authority explicit and redistributing it across the design process.
pages.title: Make the Invisible Visible (Power Dynamics)

pages.description: A systematic process for identifying the gap between current and desired performance and determining whether instruction is the right remedy.
pages.title: Needs Analysis

pages.description: Deriving a course's goal tree from an external framework — a standards set, competency model or certification blueprint — and carrying the framework's own codes through objectives, activities and assessment items so that coverage and provenance stay traceable in both directions.
pages.title: Standards Crosswalk

pages.description: A systematic method for breaking down a complex skill or task into its component knowledge, skills, and decision points so instruction can be designed around what learners actually need to master.
pages.title: Task Analysis

pages.description: 4C/ID is a design pattern for teaching complex skills by organizing instruction around four coordinated components: whole learning tasks, supportive information, procedural information, and part-task practice.
pages.title: 4C/ID (Four-Component Instructional Design)

pages.description: The 5E Learning Cycle organizes instruction into five phases — Engage, Explore, Explain, Elaborate, Evaluate — sequencing hands-on exploration before formal explanation.
pages.title: 5E Learning Cycle

pages.description: Adaptive learning is the short-form canonical pattern for adjusting pacing, difficulty, or support based on learner performance.
pages.title: Adaptive Learning

pages.description: A dedicated, ungraded, choice-rich block of school time built around a library of leveled STEAM challenges, peer expertise, and observing (not directing) facilitators — designed to make genuine interest-driven learning possible within, not just outside, the school day.
pages.title: Alternative In-School STEAM Learning Infrastructure

pages.description: Anchored instruction organizes learning around a rich, shared scenario that acts as the \"anchor\" for inquiry, discussion, and problem solving.
pages.title: Anchored Instruction

pages.description: Authentic assessment evaluates learning through tasks that mirror the knowledge work of real disciplines, professions, and communities rather than through proxies like multiple-choice tests.
pages.title: Authentic Assessment

pages.description: A progressive, multi-institution making project design that uses living-organism art materials and low-threshold, self-buildable tools to move learners across art, science, and nature-facing institutional boundaries.
pages.title: Bioart Boundary-Crossing Making

pages.description: Blended Learning is the pattern-level target for instruction that intentionally combines in-person and digital learning experiences so each mode does some work the other does not.
pages.title: Blended Learning

pages.description: A group activity in which learners physically build a large geometric structure from manipulatives using only a target image and a list of properties (no assembly instructions), forcing iterative discovery and naming of structural constraints.
pages.title: Body-Scale Collaborative Geometric Construction

pages.description: Case-based learning is the short-form canonical pattern for learning through analysis of realistic cases.
pages.title: Case-Based Learning

pages.description: Case-based learning in the Harvard method uses a carefully written case as the center of discussion, analysis, and decision making.
pages.title: Case-Based Learning (Harvard Method)

pages.description: CGI for Math is the short-form canonical target for Cognitively Guided Instruction in mathematics, where instruction is built around learners' informal strategies and explanation of problem solving.
pages.title: CGI for Math

pages.description: Cognitive apprenticeship adapts the structure of traditional craft apprenticeship to the teaching of complex cognitive skills.
pages.title: Cognitive Apprenticeship

pages.description: Cognitive Flexibility Theory is a pattern for teaching in ill-structured domains by repeatedly revisiting concepts across multiple cases, perspectives, and contexts.
pages.title: Cognitive Flexibility Theory

pages.description: This pattern designs instruction to reduce unnecessary load while preserving the mental work that actually contributes to learning.
pages.title: Cognitive Load Reduction (CLT Scaffolding Approach)

pages.description: Cognitive Load Theory is the short-form canonical target for CLT-informed instructional patterns that reduce extraneous load and calibrate support to expertise.
pages.title: Cognitive Load Theory

pages.description: CGI for math is a pattern in which instruction begins with learners' own mathematical thinking and strategies rather than with a fixed demonstration of one correct method.
pages.title: Cognitively Guided Instruction (CGI) for Math

pages.description: Collaborative evaluation is a pattern in which learners assess resources, proposals, performances, or solutions together using shared criteria.
pages.title: Collaborative Evaluation

pages.description: Collaborative inquiry is a pattern in which learners pose questions together, investigate possible answers, critique emerging explanations, and revise their understanding in public.
pages.title: Collaborative Inquiry

pages.description: Collaborative learning is the short-form canonical pattern for shared work, discussion, and co-construction of understanding.
pages.title: Collaborative Learning

pages.description: Competency-Based Learning is a pattern that organizes progression around demonstrated competence on defined outcomes rather than uniform pacing.
pages.title: Competency-Based Learning

pages.description: Students investigate a disciplinary question by extending a provided code simulation and writing a computational essay — a document mixing prose, executable code, and visualization — to explain their question, method, and findings to peers.
pages.title: Computational Essay Writing

pages.description: Learners infer the defining attributes of a concept by comparing labeled positive and negative examples, then test and refine their hypothesis.
pages.title: Concept Attainment

pages.description: Constructive alignment coordinates intended learning outcomes, teaching activities, and assessment tasks so that what learners are asked to do, practice, and be graded on all demand the same cognitive work.
pages.title: Constructive Alignment

pages.description: Cooperative learning structures small-group work so that members are positively interdependent, individually accountable, and taught explicit collaborative skills.
pages.title: Cooperative Learning

pages.description: A multi-month, community-based STEM making program in which youth identify locally-rooted problems through ethnography, prototype solutions with iterative community feedback, and present at a public entrepreneurial platform while reframing "entrepreneurship" toward community benefit rather than profit or competition.
pages.title: Critical Maker-Entrepreneurialism Program

pages.description: A three-stage pattern that builds learners' data-storytelling and critical-data-literacy skills by moving from analyzing existing data stories, to remixing an exemplary one, to authoring and performing an original one with open data.
pages.title: Data Storytelling — Forage, Remix, DIY

pages.description: Debate is the short-form canonical pattern for structured instructional argumentation around a contested question.
pages.title: Debate

pages.description: Debate format is a structured discussion pattern in which learners prepare positions, present arguments, respond to opposing claims, and justify conclusions within a defined sequence.
pages.title: Debate Format

pages.description: Develop Understanding is a lesson-scale pattern that moves learners from initial exposure to meaningful conceptual grasp by activating prior knowledge, introducing new ideas clearly, giving guided opportunities to use them, and then…
pages.title: Develop Understanding

pages.description: When a participatory or deliberative process fails to sustain an underrepresented group's engagement despite outreach and translation, redesign the activity's own tools, norms, and division of labor — a dedicated deliberative space, native-language deliberation instead of sequential interpretation, and flexible agendas — rather than adding more interpretation or outreach to the existing structure.
pages.title: Differentiated Activity Structures for Inclusive Participation

pages.description: Direct instruction is the short-form canonical pattern for explicit explanation, modeling, guided practice, and feedback.
pages.title: Direct Instruction

pages.description: Discussion-Based Learning is a pattern in which understanding is built through structured conversation rather than one-way presentation alone.
pages.title: Discussion-Based Learning

pages.description: Discussion Group is a structured pattern for using small-group or whole-group talk to deepen understanding, surface interpretation, and test ideas in relation to a prompt or problem.
pages.title: Discussion Group

pages.description: Elaboration Theory is the short-form canonical target for Reigeluth's elaboration pattern, which sequences from simple, inclusive ideas toward more complex detail.
pages.title: Elaboration Theory

pages.description: A session structure that pairs a short physics concept demonstration with dance improvisation exploring that concept, validating culturally specific movement styles as legitimate scientific expression.
pages.title: Embodied Physics Inquiry Through Dance Improvisation

pages.description: Emergent curriculum builds instruction from students' own expressed interests as they arise, rather than from goals set in advance by curriculum writers or teachers, requiring continuous observation and flexible responsiveness in place of predetermined planning.
pages.title: Emergent Curriculum

pages.description: Epistemic Games immerse learners in the values, identity, and situated decision-making of a professional community of practice, so that facts and skills are acquired as a byproduct of doing the community's work rather than as isolated content.
pages.title: Epistemic Games

pages.description: The experiential learning cycle organizes learning as a repeating four-stage sequence — concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualization, and active experimentation — that turns raw experience into tested knowledge.
pages.title: Experiential Learning Cycle

pages.description: A two-part unit design that first gives students a reason to engage with historical background knowledge through discussion-based case studies and source-sorting, then supports the procedural writing skill of placing and connecting that background to evidence through modeled text analysis and targeted language practice.
pages.title: Explicit Instruction in Historical Contextualization

pages.description: Explicit teaching is the short-form canonical pattern for clearly stating goals, demonstrating performance, and guiding practice.
pages.title: Explicit Teaching

pages.description: A multi-day craft camp (knitting, crochet, and fabric pleating) in which learners define their own stitch or fold units through personal tension and material choice, then discover multiplicative proportional relationships (e.g., stitch width-to-height ratios, row-to-row growth, unfolded-to-folded fabric ratios) as an emergent property of the material rather than a taught formula.
pages.title: Fiber Crafting for Proportional Reasoning

pages.description: The Five "E" Model is a constructivist lesson pattern with five sequential stages — Engage, Explore, Explain, Elaborate, Evaluate — that structures inquiry-based lessons around students' own discovery before formal terminology is introduced.
pages.title: Five "E" Model

pages.description: Flipped Classroom is a pattern that shifts some direct instruction or initial content acquisition outside class so that class time can be used for application, discussion, problem solving, and feedback.
pages.title: Flipped Classroom

pages.description: Flipped Learning is a pattern that moves some initial content exposure outside class so synchronous time can be used for application, discussion, and feedback.
pages.title: Flipped Learning

pages.description: Formative Assessment is a pattern in which instruction repeatedly cycles through eliciting evidence, interpreting it, and adjusting teaching or learning before final evaluation.
pages.title: Formative Assessment

pages.description: Fostering Communities of Learning is a pattern for organizing a class as a knowledge-building community rather than a collection of isolated learners.
pages.title: Fostering Communities of Learning (FCL)

pages.description: Gagné's 9 Events of Instruction is a structured lesson pattern that sequences attention, objectives, recall, presentation, guidance, practice, feedback, assessment, and transfer.
pages.title: Gagné's 9 Events of Instruction

pages.description: Game-Based Mastery Learning is the short-form canonical target for mastery designs that combine progression gates, repeated practice, feedback, and game-like incentives or progression signals.
